title: Feature flag service
brief: Companies turn features on and off for groups of users without redeploying. Millions of apps ask "is this on for me?", and the answer must be instant. A wrong flag value can take down an entire customer, so changes must roll out safely and be reversible in seconds.

clarify.q: Do apps ask your servers on every check?
clarify.a: No. Apps download the rules and decide locally. Your service sends the rules and receives usage reports.

clarify.q: How quick must an emergency off-switch be?
What if your service is down?
clarify.a: The app keeps using its last known rules. You must never be the cause of a customer outage.

notes: A rule file is about 50 KB for a big customer (approx.).
Usage events are small and can be a minute late.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

Usage events per second at peak
Rule data held by the CDN
numbers.how: 2,000 customers × 50 KB ≈ 100 MB, small enough to keep everywhere (approx.)

hints: Every app downloads the same file for its customer. Where can a copy of that file live?
Serve rules from a CDN with a short time to keep them, and push changes to connected apps with a socket gateway. Think about what stops a bad change.
Rollback content still needs a monotonically newer publication identity. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Rules are small and read by many, so the CDN does the heavy lifting with a short keep time. Sockets announce changes. The riskiest part is a bad change: staged rollouts, a kill switch and a last-known-good fallback keep one mistake from reaching everyone.

designs.name: CDN-first with staged changes
designs.why: Nearly every read is a CDN hit, so the origin stays calm even when thousands of apps reconnect together. Staged rollouts limit a bad change to a small share, and metrics with alerts make sure you notice fast.

tradeoffs: A shorter CDN keep time makes changes appear sooner but sends more traffic to the origin.
Pushing changes over sockets is fast but means holding millions of open connections.
Staged rollouts slow a good change down a little, and make a bad change far less costly.
Apps that fall back to the last known rules stay safe even if you are completely down.
editorial.realWorld: Flag services deliver rule changes to connected apps in well under a second and handle many billions of flag checks a day, nearly all evaluated locally (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Feature flag service: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Evaluate consistent versioned flags and roll back unsafe changes quickly. Stable cohorts let operators compare behavior and avoid flickering features. Partial rules can create contradictory decisions; publication must be atomic. Rollback content still needs a monotonically newer publication identity.

fields.label: Step 1. A user gets a 10% rollout flag on two replicas. What keeps assignment stable?
options: A stable user and flag hash with a versioned rule set
A random choice on every evaluation
fields.explanation: Stable cohorts let operators compare behavior and avoid flickering features.

fields.label: Step 2. A config update is malformed on one replica. Activate it?
options: Apply fields as they stream in
Validate a complete generation and retain the previous known-good version
fields.explanation: Partial rules can create contradictory decisions; publication must be atomic.

fields.label: Step 3. Errors breach the rollout stop threshold. What do clients do?
options: Accept a newer rollback generation and bounded cache invalidation
Ignore rollback because its payload resembles an older version
fields.explanation: Rollback content still needs a monotonically newer publication identity.

correctness.responsibility: Evaluate consistent versioned flags and roll back unsafe changes quickly.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
